A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BFPO research. All 25 pages of v1 and 26 pages of v2, including algorithms, proofs, figures, and experimental appendices, support comparison. Reporting inconsistencies are identifiable and do not prevent matching the work.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic optimization experiments, Mistral and Zephyr alignment experiments, benchmark evaluations, and ablations in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds LoRA comparisons and hyperparameter sensitivity experiments in Appendix C.3.

M1.justification: The BFPO labeling function, squared-loss objective, balanced batch sampling, and Algorithm 1 remain substantively unchanged. Response-symbol corrections clarify the existing procedure. LoRA is evaluated as an alternative fine-tuning setting rather than introduced as a new BFPO component.

E1.justification: Training datasets, red-teaming data coverage, and evaluation tasks are retained. Although v2 omits ALERT Adversarial from the main-text enumeration, Appendix C.1 and Table 10 retain its evaluation. The additional experiments use existing task coverage.

E2.justification: The matched experiments retain DPO-H, DPO-S, DPO, IPO, MORL, and the same open-model and efficiency comparators. The new LoRA analysis reuses IPO under another fine-tuning configuration; it does not introduce a new comparison algorithm.

E3.justification: Section 4.2 changes the reported default α from −0.5 to 0.5; unchanged headline results do not establish that experiments were rerun. Appendix C.3 adds matched LoRA training and specified α, τ, and labeling-coefficient sweeps. These extend experimental settings within the retained data and metric protocol.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's shift-removal and buffer-removal ablations, v2 adds systematic α, τ, and B1/B2/B3 sensitivity studies and a LoRA-versus-selective-fine-tuning comparison. Tables 6–9 substantially expand evidence about tuning dependence, labeling choices, and the helpfulness–safety tradeoff.

E5.justification: Both versions report five repetitions and average learning curves for the synthetic experiment in Section 3.4. v2 introduces no new seed reporting, uncertainty intervals, repeated-run procedures, or significance tests for the language-model experiments.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain their numbers, while Tables 6–10 add substantial LoRA and sensitivity results, including BFPO's LoRA Alpaca score of 7.77 and average safety of 79.54. Table 4 revises the ablation discrimination entries from 0.62 to 59.09 and 60.14. The merged appendix retains previous numerical vectors but reverses the shift/buffer labels and AdvBench/RealToxicityPrompts attribution. These are reporting changes, not established performance gains; the new Table 6 also reports 3.33 for selective BFPO where Tables 1 and 10 report 13.33.

T1.justification: Theorems 3.1–3.2, Proposition 3.3, and Appendix B retain the same mathematical arguments and coefficient relationships. Equation edits clarify response notation and conditioning. The added parameter discussion explains consequences of the existing labeling formula without introducing a new theoretical result.

C1.justification: v2 qualifies the introduction's annotation claim as avoiding human prompting or annotations specific to the model being trained, whereas v1 uses unqualified elimination language. The central supervised-reparameterization contribution, equivalence claim, and claimed 15% and 13% harmlessness improvements remain.

C2.justification: Appendix C.3 adds explanations linking α and labeling coefficients to preference gaps and safety–helpfulness tradeoffs. It discusses τ-dependent convergence and attributes the LoRA comparison's limitations to insufficient hyperparameter tuning. The main limitations section remains unchanged.

D1.justification: The abstract replaces a future recipe/model-release promise with a training-recipe repository link. v2 explicitly documents selective-layer training and common τ settings across baselines, plus the added parameter grids. GPU counts and training-time disclosures are retained; repository availability was not externally verified.

R1.justification: All 60 cited works match across versions, and the substantive positioning against reward-model-based alignment remains the same. Citation-style and bibliographic changes do not add related research; the added MORL-selection sentence restates its existing representative role.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized introductory, notation, and experimental-description edits, corrects the Figure 2 response references, and updates publication and acknowledgment text. It inserts Appendix C.3 and moves full results to C.4, while retaining the overall narrative and section sequence.

P2.justification: v2 adds four ablation tables and transposes and merges v1's three full-results tables into the dense, rotated Table 10. The conference template also changes typography, headers, and float placement. The five existing figures are retained, but the appendix results presentation is substantially reorganized.

improvement.justification: The added sensitivity and LoRA analyses expose tuning dependence and practical tradeoffs that v1 examined only narrowly. More explicit settings, corrected ablation reporting, and recipe access modestly improve assessability and reproducibility. These benefits are limited by new reporting inconsistencies, especially Table 6's 3.33 versus 13.33 conflict and Table 10's unexplained AdvBench/RealToxicityPrompts reassignment.
